power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Treating serious mental illness is a formidable challenge, in part because current diagnostic categories may not capture the biological processes determining treatment response.
Progress in genetics, systems neuroscience and neuroimaging has produced important mechanistic insights, yet these advances have not yielded a practical framework for precision psychiatry.

We propose Algorithmic Circuit Psychiatry (ACP) as a roadmap for precision treatment of serious mental illness, where stratification is realized at the level of algorithms: computational processes identified via clinically relevant tasks and mappable onto neural substrates.
Using psychotic spectrum disorders as a primary case study, we argue that algorithmic description may connect circuit mechanisms to clinical symptoms more effectively than isolated neural measures.

We review evidence showing how frontal thalamocortical interactions support reasoning under uncertainty, how disruption of the relevant networks produces schizophrenia-relevant behavioral signatures, and how corresponding behavioral and neural readouts may serve as algorithmic circuit biomarkers.

We then outline how these biomarkers, combined with pharmacological perturbation, support trial design logic that can yield mechanistic insights regardless of whether a trial achieves its primary endpoint.
Serious mental illness is among the most consequential sources of disability and functional loss in medicine.
Schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and severe depression account for substantial disability, loss of functioning, and burden on patients, families, and health systems (1).

text.text: Similarly, clinical care is dominated by trial-and-error, lacking objective measurements that can guide personalized treatment.

While the advances mentioned have produced powerful computational tools and promising translational concepts, many are not validated for late-stage clinical development or remain too distal from the biological processes that determine whether a given intervention engages the relevant mechanism in a particular patient.
We propose algorithmic circuit psychiatry as a roadmap for precision treatment of serious mental illness.

The central premise is that patient stratification would be anchored in structured computational operations (algorithms), implemented in identifiable circuits and adjustable by specific mechanistic perturbations.

Algorithms are inferred using clinically relevant tasks that capture major axes of variance in a patient population and formal process models that estimate impairment-driving parameters (20) (21) (22) (23) (24).

text.text: The clinical utility of such models depends on whether the resulting parameters are biologically interpretable, and sufficiently reliable to support prospective enrichment or pharmacodynamic testing.
We use psychotic spectrum disorders as the primary case study because they expose the central translational problem with unusual clarity.

Disturbances in belief formation, reasoning under uncertainty, working memory, and cognitive control are clinically consequential, mechanistically tractable, and not adequately captured by diagnosis alone.
Psychotic disorders therefore provide a test case for linking symptom-relevant computations to circuit mechanisms, biomarkers, pharmacological perturbation, and trial design.

The framework we outline, however, can be applied to mood, anxiety, and compulsivebehavior conditions, in which heterogeneous symptoms may reflect disruptions in identifiable computations and circuits.
Precision medicine transformed oncology by creating biomarkers that drove treatment selection.
It showed that clinically similar tumors can differ in treatment-relevant biological mechanisms.

Trastuzumab is an instructive example: breast cancer defined by histology alone was too broad a category, whereas HER2 amplification or overexpression identified the subgroup in which HER2-targeted therapy substantially improved clinical outcomes (28).
text.formatted: Trastuzumab is an instructive example: breast cancer defined by histology alone was too broad a category, whereas HER2 amplification or overexpression identified the subgroup in which HER2-targeted therapy substantially improved clinical outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(28)</ref>.

text.text: This was enabled by a measurement at the appropriate level which defined both disease biology and treatment sensitivity.
Psychiatry faces a more difficult challenge because cellular biology is only one of the illness-relevant levels.
A drug that targets a receptor does so within a neuron that sits within a circuit that implements a computation that propagates across a large-scale neural system.
The central challenge is therefore to identify which level of organization is most clinically informative for a particular intervention.
Several major efforts have collectively moved the field toward this goal.
The Research Domain Criteria initiative was designed with the goal of identifying dimensions of function linked to circuits and behavior to ultimately replace diagnostic categories (29, 30).

text.text: These efforts have led to major innovations and insights, but their utility for differential treatment selection has not yet been prospectively established.

Depression provides a complementary example: resting-state connectivity studies proposed neurophysiological subtypes associated with treatment response (32), whereas a subsequent methodological replication did not establish statistically significant connectivity-symptom associations or discrete clusters in an independent sample (33).

text.text: This contrast underscores the distinction between discovering candidate subgroups and validating reproducible stratification tools.

One area of progress in this domain has been the identification of post hoc stratification signals, which illustrate the promise of focusing on features that predict treatment responsiveness and ones that may signal mechanistic proximity.

For example, the recent approval of xanomeline-trospium (KarXT), the first antipsychotic acting through muscarinic receptor agonism rather than dopamine D2 receptor blockade (34), has provided a new window into patient stratification.

text.text: Together, these examples suggest that treatment response can reveal latent biology obscured by diagnostic categories.
Post hoc stratification identifies candidate features that predict treatment responsiveness.
Making this approach prospective would be augmented by generative models that specify candidate features based on mechanistic proximity.

Our thesis is that psychotic illnesses result from disruptions in algorithms critical for how people build models of the world, update them based on incoming evidence, while performing uncertainty estimation and appropriate credit assignment.
An algorithm (see Figure 1 and Box 1) in the sense used here is a structured computational process that transforms task inputs into outputs through a defined sequence of operations.
text.formatted: An algorithm (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1</ref> and Box 1) in the sense used here is a structured computational process that transforms task inputs into outputs through a defined sequence of operations.

text.text: Algorithms provide a vital and strategic level of description for psychiatry because they sit at the interface between neural activity and behavior.
On the behavioral side, they can be fit to behavioral data from subjects performing structured tasks, extracting parameters that describe behavior succinctly and quantitatively.
On the neural side, they can be modeled by neural networks solving the same tasks, identifying neural signatures that can guide biomarker development in a mechanistically proximal manner.

In Marr's terms, ACP links the algorithmic level of description to its implementational substrate, while extending that hierarchy toward clinically measurable phenotypes, pharmacological perturbation, and treatment selection (41).
text.formatted: In Marr's terms, ACP links the algorithmic level of description to its implementational substrate, while extending that hierarchy toward clinically measurable phenotypes, pharmacological perturbation, and treatment selection <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(41)</ref>.

text.text: ACP builds on recent proposals for multi-level algorithmic psychiatry (42); its specific additions are a requirement for symptom-proximal task design, a taxonomy of biomarker classes and their intended uses (Table 1), and a trial logic with prespecified decision points (Figure 1B).

text.text: However, they exhibit two major limitations.
First, many of the tasks in computational psychiatry have been adapted from cognitive science and were not explicitly designed to capture symptom-relevant behavioral variation.
Thus, although patients may exhibit fitted parameters that are different than controls, it is not always clear they are along the same axis of behavioral variation that gives rise to symptoms.
Second, many models are neither built nor parameterized to generate hypotheses regarding circuit implementation or pharmacologically modifiable neural mechanisms.

Thus, despite the clear scientific value of the current approaches in computational psychiatry, these two core knowledge gaps have limited their translation into drug development and clinical practice.
Both limitations are potentially addressable.
First, high-dimensional and ecologically valid behavioral assays can move beyond accuracy, reaction time, and binary choices toward richer measurements of symptom-relevant behavioral variation.
Second, recent developments in neural network models offer novel model forms that may be easier to map to circuit implementation (43).
text.formatted: Second, recent developments in neural network models offer novel model forms that may be easier to map to circuit implementation <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(43)</ref>.

text.text: The field has typically relied on two broad model families.
The first comprises hand-crafted and biophysical models with prespecified forms and interpretable parameters, such as Bayesian and reinforcement learning models (20) (21) (22) (23) (24).

text.text: The second comprises neural-network models that show much better fit to behavioral performance but tend to be black boxes with limited interpretability.

Recent efforts have gone into creating hybrid models, which include interpretable hand-crafted components and neural-network components with higher computational capacity (44), and neural networks constrained to remain interpretable (45).
text.formatted: Recent efforts have gone into creating hybrid models, which include interpretable hand-crafted components and neural-network components with higher computational capacity <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(44)</ref>, and neural networks constrained to remain interpretable <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(45)</ref>.

text.text: These models may be exactly what is needed to move beyond the limitations outlined above.
Quantifying this variation can also provide principled estimates of population variance and sample-size requirements for prospective trials.
ACP organizes research and treatment development around these requirements.

An algorithm is most clinically useful when it captures symptom-relevant behavior, maps onto circuit implementation with sufficient specificity, and generates testable predictions about how a treatment should alter molecular target engagement and clinical outcomes.
These links are often difficult to derive from human experiments alone because they require mechanistic granularity and causal perturbations that are often most feasible in animal experiments (18).

text.text: ACP also clarifies how animal research can contribute to psychiatric treatment development.
Traditional psychiatric neuroscience often relied on animal tasks intended to evoke behavioral features that qualitatively look like psychiatric symptoms in humans.
While such tasks have clear value (46) (47) (48), they are frequently too unconstrained to isolate a specific circuit implementation.

text.text: A behavior such as immobility, avoidance, or impaired sensorimotor gating most likely reflects many circuit implementations, which by definition limits their mapping to a specific algorithmic perturbation, limiting their translational utility.
ACP instead prioritizes cross-species tasks that impose a well-defined computational demand (18, 19, 49, 50).
text.formatted: ACP instead prioritizes cross-species tasks that impose a well-defined computational demand <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(18,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">19,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">49,</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">50)</ref>.

text.text: With the computational problem held constant, cell-type-specific recordings and manipulations in animals can clarify circuit implementation, while translational tasks in humans can assess whether the same algorithmic failure is present clinically and whether it is associated with a specific pattern of neural alterations.

To provide a concrete example, we highlight how a set of well-controlled animal tasks, coupled with neural recordings and causal manipulations, clarified how frontal thalamocortical loops between the mediodorsal thalamus and prefrontal cortex implement computations critical for flexible cognitive control (18, 19, (51) (52) (53), as reviewed elsewhere (50, 54).

text.text: This work collectively suggests that prefrontal cortex supports high-dimensional, context-dependent representations that map task inputs onto behaviorally relevant outputs (49, 50, 55), whereas the mediodorsal thalamus is required to help sustain, amplify, and flexibly reconfigure these prefrontal representations (18, 52, 53, 56, 57).

text.text: One computational account suggests that the mediodorsal thalamus extracts lower-dimensional contextual and uncertainty-related signals from prefrontal activity and uses these signals to enable more efficient learning and generalization of prefrontal representations (43, (58) (59) (60) (61).

text.text: In that way, this frontal thalamocortical system utilizes powerful architectural features of these two components: the highly recurrent prefrontal architecture for high-dimensional computations, matching arbitrary inputs to task-relevant outputs, and the feedforward thalamus, which can de-mix contextual variables for efficient control.
Together they provide a powerful system that can still rapidly switch when task demands change.
Applying the same tasks to schizophrenia patients has shown promising results in identifying an algorithmic vulnerability and a corresponding neural signature.

Specifically, in a task in which subjects are cued to select between two conflicting targets, and where cue ambiguity (sensory uncertainty) is parameterized, patients can perform roughly at an equivalent level to controls when cueing is unambiguous.
However, their performance degrades faster when sensory uncertainty is increased (62).
text.formatted: However, their performance degrades faster when sensory uncertainty is increased <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">(62)</ref>.

text.text: This algorithmiclevel change (a shift in psychometric threshold) was related to resting-state functional connectivity between the mediodorsal thalamus and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex in a subsample of participants (62), consistent with evidence that the mediodorsal thalamus regulates frontal interactions during cognitive flexibility in healthy individuals (63).

text.text: Given the animal studies outlined above, this neuroimaging readout should be considered as a candidate algorithmic neural biomarker that provides a testable hypothesis for patient enrichment.
A parallel line of work has developed another example of the ACP approach in the context of spatial working-memory (sWM) precision.

Building on animal and biophysical models in which recurrent cortical circuits maintain location-specific activity (64), computational modeling work predicted that NMDA receptor hypofunction and cortical disinhibition should broaden mnemonic spatial tuning, degrading the precision of stored spatial representations and increasing vulnerability to distractors (65).

text.text: Together, this work identifies loss of sWM precision as a candidate algorithmic phenotype and spatial tuning within the frontoparietal network as a candidate algorithmic neural readout for enrichment and pharmacodynamic testing.

Ongoing follow-up studies using more complex versions of such task paradigms, in which multiple algorithmic components can be queried, may provide a path towards stratifying patients with psychosis symptoms on the basis of jointly modeling their behavioral and neural readouts.

Overall, and in addition to establishing frontal thalamocortical networks as readouts and potential targets for interventions, this line of work highlights the utility of an algorithmic circuit approach for biomarker development.

text.text: However, restingstate connectivity is not an algorithmic biomarker.

It becomes informative for ACP when it is explicitly paired with a behavioral task and computational model that link to circuit implementation that in turn generates predictions for how task-based and resting-state biomarkers should co-vary.
Electrophysiology provides a complementary measure.

text.text: Future studies that measure both ACP-informed task-based and resting-state measures, via concurrent fMRI-EEG, will be critical to derive spatiotemporal readouts in humans that can precisely measure distinct aspects of the circuit implementation across the multilevel chain.
To get closer to psychosis symptoms, task-based algorithmic readouts need to move beyond binary choice data.
The hierarchical attentional task paradigm outlined above is promising, but it may not fully close the gap with real-world symptoms shown by patients diagnosed with schizophrenia.
To test such algorithmic phenotypes, we highlight an effort to develop a platform to measure reasoning alterations that are encountered in psychotic illness.

Here we describe a candidate framework with two key components used to build an algorithmic neural biomarker: i) a scenario-based reasoning platform that yields high-dimensional behavioral readouts, similar in spirit to bias against disconfirmatory evidence measurements (79, 80); ii) a circuit-mapped algorithmic model that connects the main computational operation the task estimates to candidate druggable targets (Figure 2; Box 2).

text.text: The scenario-based reasoning platform would present participants with individual scenarios in which they rate the plausibility of multiple interpretations and update those interpretations as the scenario unfolds.
Scenarios can be parameterized by working-memory load and uncertainty, yielding higher-dimensional behavioral readouts than binary choice data.
The task component of the platform could reveal robust reasoning deficits in schizophrenia patients as well as potential utility in monitoring treatment responsiveness.
The model would then be fit to patient data to provide candidate cellular entry points for possible correction on an individualized basis.

The model would contain parameters defining algorithmic phenotypes of belief rigidity or volatility, while generating predictions for neural readouts, enrichment, and pharmacodynamic hypotheses concerning interventions that target the implicated neural systems that map onto the pattern of computational impairments identified.
Psychiatric drug development has a recurring failure mode: when a compound fails to separate from placebo on a symptom endpoint, the trial is often difficult to interpret.

The same null result can reflect incorrect target biology, insufficient exposure or dose, inadequate target engagement, enrollment of a population without the relevant pathophysiology, excessive heterogeneity, an insensitive endpoint, or elevated placebo response.
Symptom endpoints are necessary for clinical development, but when used alone they do not identify where the translational chain failed.
For example, balovaptan did not improve the primary socialization and communication endpoint relative to placebo in a pediatric autism trial (81).

text.text: Such a null result establishes lack of benefit on the tested endpoint, but does not by itself identify which link in the proposed mechanistic chain failed.
Algorithmic circuit trial design converts this ambiguity into a structured operational sequence with prespecified decision points (Figure 1B).

text.text: A compound enters a study with a proposed molecular mechanism.
That mechanism generates a prespecified prediction about effects on cell types or microcircuit regulators.
The predicted microcircuit effect generates a systems-level prediction, such as altered thalamocortical connectivity or prefrontal oscillatory dynamics.

The predicted systems-level change generates a prediction about an algorithmic phenotype readout, such as improved uncertainty-dependent reasoning, belief updating, working memory gating, or credit assignment.
Finally, the model prespecifies whether algorithmic improvement should predict symptom or functional improvement over a clinically meaningful interval.

Establishing whether normalization of the algorithmic phenotype is necessary, sufficient, or both for clinical improvement will require analyses within existing therapeutic trials and longitudinal cohorts, followed by prospective validation.
This operational sequence creates interpretable failure points.

If a drug does not move the algo-rithmic neural biomarker, after adequate exposure has been established using prespecified PK/PD and target-engagement criteria, the result localizes failure to the target-engagement or target-to-circuit step.
If the circuit biomarker shows an effect but the algorithmic phenotype readout does not, the circuit-tocomputation model, measurement strategy, dose, or timing requires revision.

If both neural and phenotypic algorithmic readouts show effects, but there is no effect on symptom endpoints, the algorithm-to-symptom link may be weaker, slower, subgroup-specific, or insufficiently captured by the selected clinical endpoint.
A negative outcome at any step of this operational chain is more informative than a failure on a symptom endpoint alone.

Furthermore, failure at a given step can directly inform refinement of patient selection, dosing, endpoint timing, biomarker strategy, or the underlying circuit-to-algorithm model in subsequent trials.

The neural readout should index the circuit substrate hypothesized to implement the algorithm, allowing exposure, target engagement, circuit response, and algorithmic response to be evaluated as distinct links in the chain.

Each decision point therefore requires a prespecified effect-size threshold, equivalence bound, or Bayesian decision rule, together with measures of known reliability; otherwise a negative result cannot be distinguished from an underpowered measurement.

Because the sequence assumes serial mediation, whereas interventions may also act through parallel routes, discordant outcomes (for example, symptom improvement without the predicted neural response) should be prespecified as tests of the circuit model rather than of efficacy.
Patient selection is central to this framework.
If a trial enrolls many patients whose baseline circuit state is not aligned with the mechanism of action, a drug may appear ineffective even if it works in the biologically relevant subgroup.
Baseline circuit and algorithmic characterization can support prospective enrichment, stratified randomization, or predefined responder analyses.
This approach does not require that biomarkers be perfectly aligned with clinical symptom endpoints.
It requires that they be mechanistically interpretable, reproducible enough for the intended use, and specified before the trial begins.

Because algorithmic phenotypes may cut across diagnostic categories, early mechanistic studies may also benefit from cross-diagnostic enrollment or stratification while retaining conventional diagnoses for clinical interpretation and regulatory reporting.

However, enrichment strategies that resemble companion diagnostics may increase development complexity, regulatory burden, and commercial risk; these incentives should be addressed through early biomarker qualification and prospective evidence that enrichment materially improves trial efficiency or treatment benefit.
The proposed framework should also change how negative trials are valued.
A failed symptom endpoint should not automatically be treated as a failed experiment.

If the trial was designed with prespecified circuit and algorithmic readouts, it can identify whether the underlying model was wrong, the target was not engaged, the selected population was mismatched, or the clinical endpoint was insensitive.
A cumulative science of psychiatric treatment depends on learning from failure rather than repeatedly rediscovering ambiguity.

The near-term sweet spot for ACP is the transition from preclinical behavioral pharmacology to phase 2 proof-of-concept studies, where circuit and algorithmic measures can de-risk mechanism selection before late-stage development.
ACP is an aspirational biomarker platform.
Several boundary conditions are important.
Psychiatric syndromes are heterogeneous, and no single computation is likely to explain all relevant symptoms within diagnoses defined by current nosology.
Circuit readouts are state-dependent and may be influenced by medication exposure, sleep, arousal, substance use, development, and comorbidity.
Computational tasks must be reliable (84, 85), scalable, tolerable for patients, and interpretable at the individual level (86).

text.text: Algorithmic readouts must show incremental value for de-risking clinical trials beyond conventional clinical and cognitive assessments.
Any treatment-selection claim requires prospective validation in trials designed to test it.
The framework therefore imposes evidentiary requirements.

Candidate biomarkers should demonstrate measurement reliability (including test-retest reliability, parameter recovery for model-derived measures, and a minimal detectable change smaller than the expected treatment effect), sensitivity to pharmacological or behavioral perturbation (87), a demonstrable relationship to the specified computation, and relevance to clinical outcomes.
Multimodal signatures should be evaluated for whether they improve prediction beyond simpler measures.
Claims about surrogate endpoints should be avoided until supported by appropriate evidence.
In the near term, the most realistic use of algorithmic circuit biomarkers may be mechanistic enrichment and early pharmacodynamic assessment rather than definitive clinical decisionmaking.
Making these constraints explicit is what renders the framework testable.

The field does not need another vocabulary for heterogeneity; it needs a disciplined method for specifying which computation is disrupted, which circuit implements it, which intervention should modify it, and which measurement would show that the intended change occurred.
ACP is a proposed framework for making actionable progress in precision neuropsychiatry by linking circuitimplemented computations to algorithmically informed neural and phenotypic measures.
It does not argue that we replace diagnosis, symptom scales, molecular pharmacology, or any existing neural readout tool.
Instead, ACP organizes the tools the field has advanced into a causal and testable experimental sequence that can be implemented in trials.
The thalamocortical uncertainty example illustrates how this sequence can work.
A clinically meaningful computation is identified.
Animal studies clarify circuit implementation.
Human tasks measure the corresponding algorithmic phenotype.
Imaging and electrophysiology provide circuit-level readouts.
Pharmacological perturbation tests whether the mechanism changes the predicted levels of the chain.
Trial design then becomes more informative because success or failure can be localized.
Patients with serious mental illness need treatments that improve how they think, reason, decide, and function in the world.
Achieving that goal requires more than better symptom scales or more reproducible 'biotype' clusters.
It requires knowing which circuit operations are disrupted, which circuits implement them, and how to measure and target those circuits in a way that informs treatment.
Algorithmic circuit psychiatry is a proposed roadmap for building that knowledge into clinical development and, ultimately, clinical care.

text.text: Content-Aligned Gain of Evidence (CAGE) as an ACP implementation example.
A. Scenario-based reasoning task.
Participants rate competing interpretations as sequential scenario evidence unfolds.
Plausibility ratings (0-100) are made independently for each interpretation and need not sum to 100.

Evidence updates can vary in reliability and in whether they confirm or disconfirm the participant's current interpretation, providing a symptom-proximal reasoning platform for estimating algorithmic phenotypes.
B. Content-dependent evidence gain.
The Content-Aligned Gain of Evidence model formalizes the hypothesis that incoming evidence may be weighted according to its alignment with the current belief.
Positive alignment means prior-congruent evidence; negative alignment means prior-incongruent evidence.
This is agreement versus disagreement, not correct versus incorrect evidence.
Evidence can support a false belief.
Prior-congruent evidence is governed by confirmatory amplification strength, whereas prior-incongruent evidence is governed by disconfirmatory suppression strength.
A normative reference corresponds to evidence receiving its nominal weight, indicating no content-dependent amplification or suppression.

The model is motivated by predictionerror accounts of psychosis (88) (89) (90) (91) (92), including dual-pathway formulations in which positive and negative prediction-error signals may differentially contribute to belief volatility and rigidity (93).

The black curve shows a reference parameterization; the orange dashed curve shows an amplification-dominant parameter profile, and the blue dashed curve shows a suppression-dominant profile.
None of the three curves is flat: each varies with alignment, so none coincides with the normative reference of uniform, content-independent weighting.
The gain function multiplies the nominal reliability of the evidence, thereby changing the influence of evidence on subsequent belief updating.
C. Belief lock-in simulation.
Inference step 0 denotes the initial belief; subsequent steps denote successive evidence updates.

All three trajectories share the same initial belief, initial prior precision, prior-precision reinforcement and evidence sequence, and differ only in the gain function: the blue trajectory uses the suppression-dominant profile and the orange trajectory the amplification-dominant profile drawn in Panel B, while the grey trajectory uses content-independent gain.
Belief-biased perception is switched off in this panel so that the comparison isolates content-dependent gain (Box 2).

Evidence consists of a brief noise-seeded confirming onset followed by sustained evidence of mixed sign whose mean is zero, so the true state is zero throughout; tick marks along the lower edge show the sign of each evidence sample.
The content-independent trajectory tracks the truth.
The suppression-dominant trajectory holds its false belief through runs of disconfirming evidence.
The amplification-dominant trajectory releases the belief under disconfirmation and re-captures it when confirming evidence returns.
The preliminary simulation applies the gain rule from Panel B to repeated belief updating.
The update weight depends on the effective reliability of the evidence after content-dependent gain has been applied.
Therefore, belief-congruent evidence can exert greater influence, whereas disconfirmatory evidence can exert reduced influence.
Beliefs are updated by shifting the current belief toward the new evidence in proportion to that update weight, where the discrepancy between evidence and belief is the prediction error (Box 2).
This produces trajectories ranging from flexible correction toward truth to rigid lock-in or amplification-dominant capture.
The model is illustrative rather than a definitive model of delusions.
Box 2 provides an expanded description of this example algorithmic phenotype model.
D. ACP implementation logic.
The same parameters can be treated as candidate algorithmic phenotypes for translational studies.

Elevated confirmatory amplification indexes excessive weighting of belief-congruent evidence, whereas elevated disconfirmatory suppression indexes excessive down-weighting of disconfirmatory evidence.

These phenotypes can be estimated from reasoning-task behavior, mapped to hypothesized neural biomarkers, and tested prospectively as enrichment, stratification, or pharmacodynamic readouts in Algorithmic Circuit Psychiatry studies.
Box 2 defines all model parameters and reports the parameter values used in each panel.

Algorithm: a structured computational process that transforms inputs into outputs through formalizable operations such as evidence integration, uncertainty estimation, belief updating, working memory maintenance, or credit assignment.
Circuit implementation: the neural architecture and dynamics that realize an algorithm through coordinated signaling across cells, microcircuits, and distributed large-scale systems.

Algorithmic phenotype: an individual-level pattern of task performance, quantitatively summarized by model-derived parameters, that indexes variation in a specified computational operation and can be linked to a hypothesized circuit implementation.

Algorithmic neural biomarker: a central nervous system readout, such as an MRI-based, electrophysiological, or multimodal measure, that indexes a circuit implementation linked to an algorithmic phenotype and changes in a computationally predictable direction after perturbation of a mechanism involved in those circuits.

Treatment-selection biomarker: a baseline neuro-phenotypic measure used prospectively to enrich a trial or guide treatment selection because it identifies patients whose circuit state is aligned with the proposed mechanism of action.

Algorithmic Circuit Psychiatry (ACP): a translational framework that uses clinically relevant tasks and formal computational models to identify algorithmic phenotypes, link them to circuit implementations, and use the resulting behavioral and neural readouts to guide patient stratification, pharmacodynamic assessment, and treatment selection.
Beliefs are updated by combining prior expectations with new evidence.

In flexible inference, new evidence should influence belief according to its reliability: more reliable evidence should produce larger updating, and less reliable evidence should produce smaller updating.
However, in symptom-relevant reasoning, evidence may also be weighted according to whether it agrees with the interpretation that is already forming.
This is the core idea of the Content-Aligned Gain of Evidence (CAGE) model illustrated in Figure 2B-C.

This creates a positive feedback loop.
A weak false belief may initially arise from noise or ambiguous evidence.
If early evidence happens to support that false belief, the model amplifies its impact.
The belief then becomes stronger.
Once the belief is stronger, later evidence is evaluated relative to that strengthened belief.
Evidence that supports the belief receives greater influence, whereas evidence that contradicts the belief has less influence.
Over repeated updates, this process can produce belief lock-in: the belief becomes resistant to correction even when the true state would otherwise support revision.

The simulation in Figure 2C illustrates three belief trajectories that differ only in gain: i) A content-independent trajectory tracks the truth because evidence is weighted without regard to whether it confirms or disconfirms the current belief; ii) A suppression-dominant trajectory locks in: strong suppression of disconfirmatory evidence prevents runs of disconfirmation from reducing the belief, while prior-precision accumulation on each confirmation progressively hardens it; iii) An amplification-dominant trajectory shows volatile capture: weaker suppression lets disconfirming runs pull the belief back toward the truth, after which strong amplification of the next confirming evidence re-captures it.

text.text: Across repeated evidence sequences, the suppression-dominant profile settles on a stable false belief in essentially every run, whereas the amplification-dominant profile does so in only a minority of runs; this lock-in requires both disconfirmation suppression and prior-precision accumulation, and neither produces it alone.
These trajectories should not be interpreted as a definitive computational model of delusions.
Instead, they illustrate how a simple, clinically interpretable evidence-weighting mechanism can generate belief rigidity or amplification-dominant capture.
In that sense, the goal of this simulation was to illustrate one form of an actionable computational phenotype that maps onto Algorithmic Circuit Psychiatry.
Specifically, the model proposes a symptom-relevant computation, identifies measurable behavioral parameters, and proposes candidate circuit-level interpretations.
Elevated g + can be treated as an algorithmic phenotype reflecting excessive amplification of belief-congruent evidence.
Elevated g - can be treated as an algorithmic phenotype reflecting excessive suppression of disconfirmatory evidence.

These parameters can be estimated from a scenario-based reasoning task, linked to hypothesized neural systems such as salience/gain circuits (100) and prefrontal-thalamocortical precision-control systems (51, 58), and tested prospectively as enrichment or pharmacodynamic readouts.

text.text: These mappings are hypotheses; in particular, dopaminergic amplification of prediction errors of both signs would predict belief volatility rather than congruence-selective amplification (93), so the proposed link between g + and striatal salience systems requires direct testing.

Applying CAGE to the scenario-based task will also require an observation model that maps plausibility ratings over competing interpretations onto belief and evidence variables, and parameter-recovery analyses showing that g + , g -, κ, π prior , and ρ are separately identifiable under the proposed task manipulations.
The model does not replace existing computational theories of delusions.
However, it provides a concrete ACP implementation: symptomrelevant behavior is formalized as an algorithm, mapped to candidate neural mechanisms, and made testable in translational studies.
The key contribution of this formulation is a signed decomposition.

Content-dependent weighting is resolved into two separately parameterized quantities -amplification of belief-congruent evidence (g + ) and attenuation of belief-incongruent evidence (g -) -each with a distinct candidate circuit substrate, so that two individuals with indistinguishable aggregate rigidity may still differ in which gain is abnormal, and therefore in which mechanism an intervention should target.

Prior work has established this underlying asymmetry: valence-dependent learning rates are well established in reinforcement learning (94), circular inference produces functionally similar over-weighting through message reverberation (95, 96), and belief-congruent amplification has been derived as a consequence of approximate hierarchical inference (101).

text.text: The CAGE formulation adds a separation of the two directions into independently estimable parameters intended for stratification and hypothesis testing of potential interventions in the context of ACP.
There are three limitations that should be noted.

First, the lock-in shown in Figure 2C is a joint property of disconfirmation suppression and prior-precision accumulation: with κ = 0 no gain profile sustains a false belief, and with content-independent gain no amount of precision accumulation does.

text.text: The phenotype axis is therefore g -in combination with κ rather than g -alone, and the two will need to be estimated jointly or decomposed in future work.

Second, whether a false belief stabilizes depends on the statistics of the evidence as much as on the parameters: under low-amplitude evidence that never saturates alignment, every profile decays toward the truth, and only sustained evidence of both signs at sufficient magnitude engages the suppression pathway.

This is a constraint on task design -disconfirmations must be strong and must arrive before precision has accumulated -rather than a deficiency of the model, but it means that estimates of g -from tasks lacking such evidence will be uninformative.
Third, the simulation is illustrative rather than fitted, and no parameter has been estimated from human data.
The stable false states produced here are a pair of attractors symmetric about the truth.

The key aspects that remain to be tested are whether i) the depth of the attractors, ii) their resistance to perturbation, and iii) the hysteresis between formation and resolution match the phenomenology of established delusions.
Finally, connecting attractor depth to excitation-inhibition balance in biophysical models is the natural next step.
